title: Muslim at work and school
hook: You can pray at work or school without making it a big scene. Most of it is planning and one calm conversation.

screens.text: Being the only Muslim at work or school can feel like a spotlight. It doesn't have to be. A little planning and one calm conversation solve most of it.
**Plan the prayers in your day.** Each prayer has a set window [Q 4:103], usually a few hours. At work or school that's mostly **Dhuhr** and maybe **Asr**, about 5–10 minutes each with wudu.

screens.prompt: Which prayers land in your workday?
screens.text: Drag through a day and stop at your work or school hours. For most people, that's Dhuhr and maybe Asr.

steps.text: Find the gap in your schedule: a break, lunch, a free period
Find a clean, quiet spot: an empty office, a storage room, a clean spot beside your parked car
Keep a small mat or a clean jacket to pray on

screens.text: **Your rights (US).** Under **Title VII** of the Civil Rights Act, employers with 15+ workers must reasonably accommodate religious practice (prayer breaks, schedule swaps, hijab, beards) unless it causes the business substantial hardship.
bubbles: The **EEOC** enforces it, and retaliation is illegal.
{teen}Public schools generally let students pray in free time like lunch [US Dept. of Education]. If your parents don't know you're Muslim yet, talk to {{mentor.name}} first.{/teen}

screens.situation: Luis works retail. Dhuhr starts at 1:15, but his lunch break is at 11:30 and the floor gets busy after 1.

options.text: Ask his manager to move his break to about 1:30, or for a 10-minute break then
options.feedback: Yes. A specific, small request is easy to say yes to, and the law backs it.

options.text: Pray Dhuhr at 11:30 to save trouble
options.feedback: Not quite. A prayer isn't valid before its time starts. Ask for a break inside the window instead.

options.text: Sneak off for ten minutes without telling anyone
options.feedback: Risky. If someone notices you missing, it can look like slacking. A quick conversation protects you.

screens.title: How to ask
screens.intro: Keep it short, specific and friendly.

steps.text: Say what you need: "a 10-minute break around 1:30 to pray."
Show how it works for them: "I'll use my regular break time" or "I'll make up the minutes."
Ask, don't demand. If they hesitate, offer to try it for two weeks
If it goes badly, write down what was said and talk to {{mentor.name}}

screens.character: Dana, your manager (or, if you're a student, Ms. Rivera, your teacher)
screens.setup: You've asked for a quick word after a meeting. Dana is busy and a bit distracted: "Sure, what's up? I've got five minutes."
screens.goal: Ask for a short daily prayer break (or a quiet place to pray at school) clearly, and agree on a plan.
screens.success_looks_like: You state what you need in one or two sentences, offer a way it works for them, answer a question calmly, and end with a clear plan (time, place).
screens.coach_notes: Dana is reasonable but practical. She asks one or two real questions: "How long does it take?", "Where would you even do that?", "What if we're slammed?" She can hesitate but never mocks or threatens. If the convert gives a specific, flexible request, she agrees to try it. Debrief: one strength, one phrase to sharpen, and a reminder to follow up in writing (a short email or text) if it's a job.

screens.text: **Handshakes.** Many scholars hold that Muslims shouldn't shake hands with the opposite sex; some allow it where there's no desire, especially at work. Scholars differ, so ask your imam what to do in your situation.
bubbles: A simple, friendly option: smile, put your hand on your heart and say, "Nice to meet you. I don't shake hands, but it's great to meet you."

screens.prompt: At a job interview, the interviewer (opposite sex) holds out a hand. What's a good default?

options.text: Smile, hand on your heart, and greet them warmly
options.feedback: Right. It's polite and clear. Ask your imam about your own situation, since scholars differ.

options.text: Stare at the hand and say nothing
options.feedback: Not quite. Silence can feel rude. A warm greeting does the job and keeps the mood friendly.

options.text: Explain the whole ruling before answering any questions
options.feedback: Not quite. Keep it short. A smile and one friendly sentence is enough.

screens.text: Get set to pray at work or school.
steps: Check which prayers fall in your day
screens.optional_extra: If you need a break moved, write two sentences you'd say to your manager or teacher.

screens.text: Know which prayers fall in your day, have a spot, and ask for what you need in one short, friendly request.
Every prayer you fit into a busy day counts.

prayerPhrase.arabic: السَّلاَمُ عَلَيْنَا وَعَلَى عِبَادِ اللَّهِ الصَّالِحِينَ
prayerPhrase.meaning: Peace be on us, and on all of Allah's righteous servants
prayerPhrase.when: Tashahhud part 3, right after "…wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh". The Prophet ﷺ said this greeting reaches every righteous servant of Allah in the heavens and on earth [Bukhari 831]. Even alone at your desk, you're greeting a huge company.

check.prompt: Dhuhr starts at 1:15 and your break is at 11:30. What's the best move?

options.text: Ask for a short break inside Dhuhr's window
options.feedback: Right. A prayer can't be prayed before its time begins, so ask for a break that fits.
Not quite. A prayer prayed before its time isn't valid.

check.prompt: In the US, which law requires most employers to reasonably accommodate prayer?

options.text: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act (enforced by the EEOC)
options.feedback: Right. It covers employers with 15 or more workers, unless the request causes substantial hardship.
Not quite. Title VII protects religious practice at work, including prayer and dress.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Each prayer has a set time [Q 4:103]; a prayer can't be prayed before its time begins. At work or school, Dhuhr and Asr are the usual ones to plan.
- Title VII (US): employers with 15+ employees must reasonably accommodate religious practice (prayer time, schedules, dress, grooming) unless it would cause undue hardship, which since *Groff v. DeJoy* (2023) means a substantial burden in the context of the business. Retaliation is illegal. Charges go to the EEOC, usually within 180 days [EEOC].
- Public schools: students may pray during non-instructional time, such as lunch, as long as it isn't disruptive [US Department of Education guidance, 2023].
- Handshakes with the opposite sex: the majority of scholars say no (some Hanafis and Hanbalis allow it with the elderly where there's no desire); Dar al-Ifta Egypt allows following the view that permits a handshake without desire, especially in non-Muslim countries; Mathabah (Hanafi) suggests the hand-on-heart greeting at work. Teach the alternative and route the personal decision to the imam [SCHOLAR: Q9].
- Prayer phrase: tashahhud part 3 [Bukhari 831].

**Likely questions**
- *"Help me write an email."* 3–4 sentences: the request, the timing, how it works for the employer, thanks. No legal threats in a first request.
- *"My manager said no."* Ask if there's a different time or place that works. Keep notes. Suggest talking to HR, then their mentor. For legal advice, point to CAIR's legal help or an employment lawyer; don't give legal advice.
- *"Can I pray in a car or sitting down?"* Beside a parked car on a clean mat, facing the qibla, is fine; the car seat usually isn't, since obligatory prayers need standing, bowing and prostration (Day 5). Praying sitting is only for real inability, not convenience; escalate edge cases to the imam.
- *"What if the window closes before my break?"* Help them plan; if they truly can't, ask the imam. Never present skipping or delaying as normal.

**Escalate:** a job that refuses all prayer; a school that forbids prayer; a teen whose parents don't know (to {{mentor.name}}); the personal handshake decision (Q9).

**Don't**
- Don't give legal advice; point to the EEOC, CAIR or a lawyer.
- Don't suggest praying before the time starts.
- Don't suggest joining Dhuhr and Asr together to get around work. The Hanafi school doesn't allow it outside Hajj, and other schools allow it only in narrow cases; send it to the imam.
- Don't present a handshake ruling as settled either way.

**Role-play brief:** Dana is a busy, practical manager (or Ms. Rivera, a teacher). Asks real questions, may hesitate, never mocks. Agrees to a specific, flexible request. Debrief: one strength, one sharper phrase, follow up in writing.
